extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Victorian humorous sketches / readers of Charles Dickens
extracted.subtask_description: Short, comic social sketches (Victorian-era) portraying types of people and domestic scenes with satirical commentary and prescriptive asides about manners and marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal young gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Our respectful advice to the young ladies is, to seek for a young gentleman who unites in himself the best qualities of all, and the worst weaknesses of none, and to lead him forthwith to the hymeneal altar, whether he will or no.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial recommendation (satirical) that no single named 'type' is wholly recommendable; prefer a composite who combines best qualities and lacks common weaknesses. Accompanied by tongue-in-cheek procedural note: 'we are ready to receive sealed offers containing a full specification of age, temper, appearance, and condition' (i.e., specify suitor details when proposing). Also followed by a quoted practical marital admonition (Dean Swift) about preserving a husband's esteem by cultivating durable qualities to replace youth and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the young ladies' young gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: A vain, flirtatious figure who hums airs, boasts of dances 'with a lovely heiress', wins gloves by trickery, arranges his hair, accepts rosebuds and attention, and is profusely decked with scarfs, ribands, flowers, and other pretty spoils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: he eats from ladies' plates, drinks from their glasses, warbles music in praise of female loveliness, allows parasol, hat, and neck-cloth to be attended; wins gloves from sleeping young ladies; captures rosebuds after a mock skirmish. Implicit anti-patterns: vanity, theatrical affectation, playing to an audience rather than genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of an ideal wedding breakfast / festival scene
rubrics_metrics.description: A breakfast table 'glittering with plate and china', set out with flowers and sweets, long-necked bottles, and a central cake 'glistening with frosted sugar' and garnished—symbols of sumptuosity and celebration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete details used as markers of a successful, appealing wedding morning: abundant food and drink, decorative cake (Cupid or heart motifs suggested), well-dressed guests including an affluent unmarried aunt, children placed among guests in honour. Emotional indicators: tears turning to smiles, convivial merriment, and an animated send-off (carriages, waving handkerchiefs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits and behaviour of the formal couple
rubrics_metrics.description: Their faces, voices, dress, house, furniture, walk, and manner are the essence of formality; everything resolves into matter of form—they attend events to show how they are, not to see how you are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative behaviours: punctual, mechanical attendance at funerals and social rituals; exact pitch of voice, sombre look, and melancholy gait at funerals; hyper-attention to etiquette minutiae (feathers, plum-cake, port); tendency to view acquaintances as props for self-display; avoidance or censoriousness of public amusements like the theatre or exhibitions. Family effects: children become little pale, precise 'models'—a comic anti-pattern of over-brought-up youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits and behaviour of the loving (over-affectionate) couple
rubrics_metrics.description: A couple always in a loving state before company—constantly tender, affectionate and demonstrative to the point of being 'well-nigh intolerable' to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: effusive pet names and mutual commands ('Augusta, my soul' / 'Augustus, my life'), public slaps and kisses that alternate with declarations of hate/affection, and overwrought responses to minor accidents (wife repeatedly cries 'Is he dead?'). Scene examples show how continuous public display of affection can embarrass company and become comic excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescriptive marital counsel (quote from Dean Swift)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The grand affair of your life will be, to gain and preserve the esteem of your husband... You have but a very few years to be young and handsome in the eyes of the world; and as few months to be so in the eyes of a husband who is not a fool...unless you can supply the loss of youth and beauty with more durable qualities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit advice quoted and endorsed in part: women should cultivate durable qualities (virtue, good sense) to maintain their husband's esteem over time; warns against relying solely on youth and beauty. Presented in the narrative as practical, if somewhat sardonic, guidance for married women.
